# Results — Study 515 (Earnings-Announcement Premium)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim — **Frazzini–Lamont (2007)
/ Beaver (1968): a disproportionate share of a stock's total return is earned in the few days
*around* its scheduled earnings announcement** — tested on a fixed **30-name large-cap basket**.
For every trading day we tag whether it sits inside an announcement window `[D−1, D+1]` and
compare the mean daily return on announcement days against the rest, with a within-name
per-event baseline, a Welch t, a random-calendar placebo, a share-of-return decomposition, and a
tradable long-the-announcers overlay net of costs. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. **Distinct from PEAD ([../363-pead-drift](../363-pead-drift)):
that is the *drift after a surprise*; this is the *level premium on the announcement days
themselves*, irrespective of surprise sign.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Real tape | yfinance daily adjusted closes + `Ticker.get_earnings_dates` — 30 long-listed US large-caps (public, no key) |
| Window | 2005-01-03 → 2026-06-26 (**21.5** years; price tape 5,404 days × 30 names) |
| Earnings dates | **2,987** scheduled prints; **2,609** usable announcement windows |
| Announcement window | `[D−1, D+1]` trading days around each print — **4.79%** of all stock-days |
| Premium / entry / costs | per-day announce vs rest; within-name baseline; tradable overlay enters one day ahead of a *known scheduled* date (no look-ahead), one round trip/window at **2–10 bps** one-way |

> **Survivorship (named on the Signal axis).** The basket is 30 names that are *still trading*
> in 2026. A fixed surviving-names panel cannot include firms delisted or destroyed after a bad
> print, which tilts *every* leg mildly up. If anything this biases the announcement premium
> *upward* (we keep the names that survived their earnings) — and we *still* find essentially no
> premium, so the survivorship bias works against our (null) conclusion, not for it. We say so.

## The signal — return on announcement-window days vs the rest

The premium is the pooled mean daily return on announce-window days minus the rest. The Welch
*t* compares the two pools (unequal variance); the **per-event** *t* is a one-sample *t* of each
window's mean-minus-own-baseline against 0 (so cross-name level differences cancel). The placebo
*p* is the share of 20,000 **random same-density calendar tags** whose announce-minus-rest gap
**beats** the observed one.

| measure | value |
|---|--:|
| announce-day mean | **+6.33 bps/day** (n = 7,767) |
| rest-day mean | **+5.80 bps/day** (n = 154,323) |
| **premium (announce − rest)** | **+0.53 bps/day** |
| Welch *t* (announce vs rest) | **+0.16** |
| per-event premium | **−0.36 bps/day** |
| per-event one-sample *t* | **−0.11** (n = 2,609 windows) |
| placebo *p* (random calendar) | **0.394** |

Read it plainly. On the tradable `[D−1, D+1]` window the announcement premium is **+0.53 bps/day**
— statistically **indistinguishable from zero** (Welch *t* = 0.16), the within-name per-event
premium is in fact slightly **negative** (*t* = −0.11), and a random calendar of the same density
beats the observed gap **39%** of the time. **There is no announcement premium here.** Whatever
extra return earnings days carry on the broad cross-section does not show up on a liquid large-cap
survivor basket over 2005–2026.

## Share of return — announcement days carry *less* than their share

If the legend held, the ~5% of days that are announcement days should carry *much more* than 5%
of the cumulative return. They don't:

| | share of **days** | share of cumulative log **return** | concentration ratio |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| window `[D−1, D+1]` | 4.79% | **2.38%** | **0.50×** |

Announcement-window days carry only **half** their proportional share of return — the *opposite*
of the "disproportionate share" claim on this basket. The legend is **busted** at the tradable
window.

## The one honest nuance — the announcement *day itself*

Narrow the window to the single announcement day (`[D−0, D+0]`) and a faint day-of bump appears:

| window | premium | Welch *t* | per-event *t* | placebo *p* | ann-day share | concentration |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **`[D−0, D+0]`** | **+5.53 bps/day** | **+0.90** | **+0.90** | **0.052** | 1.59% | **1.45×** |
| `[D−1, D+1]` | +0.53 | +0.16 | −0.11 | 0.394 | 4.79% | 0.50× |
| `[D−2, D+2]` | +0.91 | +0.42 | +0.18 | — | 7.99% | — |

On the announcement day *alone*, the stock earns **+11.3 bps** vs **+5.7 bps** on a normal day —
roughly **double**, a 1.45× return concentration, placebo *p* = 0.052. That is the real
Frazzini–Lamont shape (the premium is *concentrated on the day*), but it is **a whisper, not a
signal**: even at its sharpest it reaches only **Welch *t* = 0.90**, far below the desk's **t ≥ 2**
bar, and it **dissolves to nothing** the moment you widen to a window you could actually trade
around (the `±1`-day window is +0.53 bps at *t* = 0.16). The directionally-correct day-of bump is
why this lands **Weak-leaning-None**, not flatly None — but it never clears the bar.

## Tradability — long the announcers, net of costs

A long-only overlay that holds the basket equal-weighted only inside announcement windows
(entered one day ahead of the *scheduled, known* date — no look-ahead), one round trip per window:

| one-way cost | gross daily | net daily | buy & hold daily | net annualised | B&H annualised |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 2 bps | +6.33 bps | **+5.00 bps** | +5.83 bps | +13.4% | +15.8% |
| 5 bps | +6.33 bps | **+3.00 bps** | +5.83 bps | +7.8% | +15.8% |
| 10 bps | +6.33 bps | **−0.34 bps** | +5.83 bps | −0.8% | +15.8% |

Even **gross**, the overlay's in-window daily return (**+6.33 bps**) barely beats always-invested
buy & hold (**+5.83 bps**) — and the overlay is in-market only ~5% of the time, so on a
*time-weighted* basis it earns a fraction of B&H. Net of a realistic round trip every window it
**underperforms buy & hold at every cost level** and turns **negative at 10 bps**. There is
nothing to deploy: the "premium" is too thin to clear its own turnover, and you would have given
up the other 95% of days that B&H collects for free.

## Synthetic positive control — the engine is faithful

On a deterministic panel where we **plant** a known extra return on the tagged announcement days,
the detector behaves exactly as it must:

| planted edge | premium (announce − rest) | Welch *t* | per-event *t* | placebo *p* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **+0.0 bps/day** (no premium) | −1.66 bps | −0.93 | −0.95 | 0.830 |
| **+15.0 bps/day** (large planted) | +13.35 bps | **+7.47** | **+7.58** | **0.000** |

With **no** planted premium the test sits at *t* ≈ −1 (it does not manufacture significance from
noise); a large planted premium lights up at *t* ≈ 7.5 and placebo *p* = 0. The control proves
the measurement is unbiased and *powered* — so the real-tape *t* = 0.16 (±1 window) / 0.90
(day-of) is a **genuine absence of a tradable premium**, not a detector that is too blunt to see
one.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** On the tradable `[D−1, D+1]` window the announcement premium is **+0.53
  bps/day at Welch *t* = 0.16** (per-event *t* = −0.11, placebo *p* = 0.39) — indistinguishable
  from zero, and announcement days carry only **0.50×** their share of return. The one honest
  nuance is a faint **day-of** bump (+5.5 bps, *t* = 0.90, 1.45× concentration) that has the right
  Frazzini–Lamont *shape* but never clears the **t ≥ 2** bar and **vanishes** at any tradable
  window. A powered synthetic control confirms the engine would have seen a real premium — there
  isn't one here. Carries an explicit **survivorship** caveat that, unusually, biases *toward*
  finding a premium (we kept the survivors) and we still find none.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The long-the-announcers overlay **underperforms buy & hold at every
  cost level** (net +3.0 bps/day at 5 bps vs B&H +5.8, negative at 10 bps) and is in-market only
  ~5% of the time — you sacrifice 95% of the year's return to chase a premium that isn't there.
  Nothing to deploy.
- **"Most of the return is earned around earnings"? — BUSTED.** Announcement-window days carry
  **2.38%** of cumulative return on **4.79%** of days — *half* their proportional share, the exact
  opposite of the claim. Only the single announcement day shows a >1× concentration (1.45×), and
  even that is a sub-*t*-2 whisper that the surrounding days erase.
